resposta: Marguerite Porete was born around 1250, probably in the county of Hainaut, between France and the Holy Roman Empire. She was a highly educated woman and a beguine, one of the women who lived their faith freely, without convent vows and without a husband. She wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls and was burned alive in Paris on 1 June 1310.
aprofundar: Almost everything we know about her comes from the trial records, written by those who wanted to silence her. Even so, the portrait that remains is clear: a writer who dared to think about the sacred with her own mind and in the language of the people. No authentic portrait of her exists; the images in the memorial are artistic representations. Say Marguerite memorial to open the full page, with audio in Portuguese and English.
camada3: To contemplate: they kept her accusations, not her face. What part of you does the world only know through what others say about you?

resposta: In the 1290s Marguerite wrote, in Old French, the language of the people, and not in Latin, The Mirror of Simple and Annihilated Souls. It is a dialogue between the Soul, Love and Reason. The Soul passes through seven states until it lets go of everything that is only its own and becomes transparent, like a mirror, to divine love.
aprofundar: She calls this annihilation: not the death of the person, but the end of the prison of the ego. Such a soul no longer lives out of fear of punishment or by trading favours with heaven; it lives free, because it loves. In chapter 22 she compares the free soul to the eagle, which flies higher than all other birds. For the power of that time, this freedom was the danger: whoever finds God through love no longer depends on intermediaries.
camada3: To contemplate: what would you need to let go of to become transparent like a mirror? Fear, pride, the need to be right?

resposta: Between 1296 and 1306 the bishop of Cambrai had the book burned in public in Valenciennes, in front of her. She did not obey the ban. Around 1308 she was arrested and handed over to the inquisitor of France, the Dominican William of Paris, the same man behind the trial of the Templars. She spent about a year and a half in prison and refused to take the oath or to answer.
aprofundar: Unable to question her, the inquisitors put the book on trial. They took fifteen sentences from it, the articles, and in April 1310 twenty-one theologians of the University of Paris declared them heretical. Today only three of the fifteen articles can be identified with certainty. Because she had kept spreading a book already condemned, she was declared a relapsed heretic. Earlier, three churchmen, among them Godfrey of Fontaines, a master of theology in Paris, had approved the text.
camada3: To contemplate: her silence was her defence. When is silence stronger than explaining yourself?

palavras: a mulher que sorriu na fogueira
resposta: On 1 June 1310, at the Place de Grève in Paris, where the City Hall square is today, Marguerite Porete was burned alive. She did not recant. The continuation of the chronicle of Guillaume de Nangis, written by someone with no sympathy for her, recorded that she faced death so calmly that the crowd wept.
aprofundar: About the phrase the woman who smiled at the stake: the sources speak of calm and serenity, and say the people wept; no source of the time says she smiled. The smile is a poetic reading of that peace. The beguin Guiard de Cressonessart, who tried to defend her, confessed under pressure and was sentenced to life in prison. They burned the woman; they could not burn what she had understood.
camada3: To contemplate: what kind of peace lets someone face the fire without hatred? Where does a calm come from that does not depend on what happens outside?

tema: After the fire: the nameless book
palavras: after the fire the nameless book
resposta: The book survived without her name. It was copied and translated into Latin, Italian and Middle English, and travelled through several countries, read by monks and nuns who did not know they were reading a condemned woman. Only in 1946 did the Italian historian Romana Guarnieri recognise Marguerite Porete's book in Latin manuscripts of the Vatican Library.
aprofundar: Before that, the Mirror was even attributed to other authors, and in 1927 it was printed in English as the work of an unknown French mystic, in Clare Kirchberger's edition. Six hundred and thirty-six years after the fire, she got her own name back.
camada3: To contemplate: her ideas travelled for centuries without a signature. Does a truth need the name of whoever said it to stay alive?

tema: Victims of the Inquisition: the memorial
palavras: victims of the inquisition the memorial
how many did the inquisition kill
resposta: Marguerite was not the only one. Historians estimate that the Spanish Inquisition prosecuted about one hundred and fifty thousand people and sent between three thousand and five thousand to their deaths. The Portuguese Inquisition, which also reached Brazil, burned at least one thousand one hundred and seventy-five people alive, according to Henry Charles Lea.
aprofundar: Among the victims of the Portuguese Inquisition was the Rio-born playwright Antônio José da Silva, executed in Lisbon in 1739. In Europe's witch hunts, driven by church courts and also by secular courts, Catholic and Protestant alike, between forty thousand and sixty thousand people were executed, most of them women. Historians themselves warn that these numbers are minimums: many deaths in prison and under torture were never recorded.
camada3: To contemplate: behind every number there is a name and a silenced voice. You do not need to despise believers to see this; many sincere believers were victims too. What can you do today so that no conscience is locked away?

resposta: The memorial has a text written as a tribute, as if she were speaking. Note: it is an imagined text, not a historical speech. It begins: I am Marguerite. I have no portrait; nobody painted my face. They kept only the accusations against me. But I left a mirror.
aprofundar: And it ends: My name is Marguerite, and through my name speak thousands who could not finish their sentence. Finish it for us. Think freely. Love without fear. Her real words are in the book. In chapter 6 the Soul says: Virtues, I take leave of you for evermore; now shall mine heart be more free and more in peace. And in chapter 22 the free soul is compared to the eagle, which flies higher than any other bird.
camada3: To contemplate: if you could leave a single sentence to those who come after you, what would it be?

resposta: The original book can be downloaded for free, in public-domain editions only: the fifteenth-century Chantilly manuscript, as a two-hundred-and-fifty-six-page PDF on Wikimedia Commons; the full Middle French text transcribed by Wikisource; and the medieval English translation published in 1927, on the Internet Archive.
aprofundar: The links are in the memorial, in the section The book, and in the sources of this lesson. The Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA 4.0 and is stored in the app to read offline. Modern translations are under copyright, so they are listed only as references, without files.
camada3: To contemplate: reading the original source, even slowly, is an act of freedom. Which book do you only know from what others said about it?
seguir: After the fire: the nameless book

resposta: Marguerite's story asks each of us: who has the right to decide what you may think, read, write and feel about the sacred? For centuries, institutions that claimed to speak in God's name used fear, fire and silence to control consciences.
aprofundar: What is denounced here is not sincere faith, but dogma armed with power, the idea that truth needs jailers. Freedom of conscience, of thought and of knowledge was won with lives like hers. Every time someone thinks for themselves, asks without fear and shares what they learned, Marguerite's flame stays lit, not as a fire, but as light.
camada3: To contemplate: on what subject do you still ask permission to think?
